title: Positional encoding
summary: Attention has no sense of order: shuffling the tokens just shuffles the outputs. So a position vector is added to each token's embedding before the first layer. It can be learned (a second table with one row per position, as in GPT-2) or fixed sine and cosine waves of many frequencies (the original transformer), where a fixed offset is a fixed rotation.
llm_link: Every LLM injects position somehow. GPT-2 adds learned position vectors, so its context length is fixed by the size of that table; many recent models use rotary position embeddings, which rotate queries and keys by a position-dependent angle inside attention.
key_ideas: Without positions, attention treats the input as a set: "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" look the same.
Input to the first layer: x_t = E[token_t] + P[t], same width d, added rather than appended.
Learned positions: a (block_size, d) table, trained like embeddings; it cannot go past its last row.
Sinusoidal positions: sin and cos pairs at geometrically spaced frequencies, like the hands of a clock.
Moving k positions forward rotates each (sin, cos) pair by a fixed angle, so relative offsets are easy to use.

quiz.q: tok_emb is (65, 32) and pos_emb is (128, 32). For a text of 10 tokens, predict the shape of tok_emb[ids] + pos_emb[:10].
quiz.explain: Both terms are (10, 32): ten rows, one per token, each of width 32. Adding keeps the width.

quiz.q: Why can a model with learned position embeddings of 1024 rows not directly read a 2000-token text?
options: There is no position vector for positions 1024 and beyond
quiz.explain: The table has exactly one row per position it was trained with. Later positions have no vector at all.

quiz.q: Predict the result: the first two entries of the sinusoidal encoding at position t = 0.
quiz.explain: sin(0) = 0 and cos(0) = 1. Every sine column is 0 and every cosine column is 1 at position 0.

quiz.q: In the clock analogy, what plays the role of the hour hand?
options: The slowest wave, which separates positions far apart
quiz.explain: Fast waves change a lot between neighbours; slow waves change only over long distances, so together they give every position a unique reading.

quiz.q: Without any positional information, what happens to a GPT's attention if you reverse the order of a prompt (ignoring the causal mask)?
options: The outputs are reversed in the same way, so word order carries no meaning
quiz.explain: Attention without positions is permutation-equivariant: permuting the inputs permutes the outputs identically. Order only matters once position vectors are added.

problems.title: Shape drill: positions and broadcasting
problems.prompt:
Predict each shape. Two of these use broadcasting: when two arrays have different shapes, NumPy stretches any axis of length 1 (or a missing leading axis) to match the other array.

a[:, None] inserts a new axis, turning a (T,) vector into a (T, 1) column.
problems.starter:
import numpy as np

V, d, T_max = 8, 6, 16
tok_emb = np.zeros((V, d))           # one row per token
pos_emb = np.zeros((T_max, d))       # one row per position
ids = np.array([3, 1, 4, 4, 0])      # a 5-token text
T = len(ids)
pos = np.arange(T)                   # positions 0..T-1
freq = np.ones(d // 2)               # one frequency per sine/cosine pair

# Predict each shape as a tuple, e.g. (4, 3), BEFORE printing anything.
# Then check yourself with print(<expression>.shape).
answers = {
    "tok_emb[ids]": None,
    "pos_emb[:T]": None,
    "tok_emb[ids] + pos_emb[:T]": None,
    "tok_emb[ids] + pos_emb[0]": None,
    "pos[:, None]": None,
    "pos[:, None] * freq[None, :]": None,
}

tests.name: shape of tok_emb[ids]
tests.code:
import numpy as np
got = answers['tok_emb[ids]']
real = np.shape(tok_emb[ids])
assert got is not None, 'fill in your prediction for tok_emb[ids]'
assert tuple(got) == tuple(real), f'you predicted {got} but tok_emb[ids] has shape {real}. Five IDs pick five rows of width d.'

tests.name: shape of pos_emb[:T]
tests.code:
import numpy as np
got = answers['pos_emb[:T]']
real = np.shape(pos_emb[:T])
assert got is not None, 'fill in your prediction for pos_emb[:T]'
assert tuple(got) == tuple(real), f'you predicted {got} but pos_emb[:T] has shape {real}. Slicing keeps the first T rows of the position table: one per position in this text.'

tests.name: shape of tok_emb[ids] + pos_emb[:T]
tests.code:
import numpy as np
got = answers['tok_emb[ids] + pos_emb[:T]']
real = np.shape(tok_emb[ids] + pos_emb[:T])
assert got is not None, 'fill in your prediction for tok_emb[ids] + pos_emb[:T]'
assert tuple(got) == tuple(real), f'you predicted {got} but tok_emb[ids] + pos_emb[:T] has shape {real}. Two (T, d) arrays add entry by entry: row t gets the embedding of token t plus position vector t.'

tests.name: shape of tok_emb[ids] + pos_emb[0]
tests.code:
import numpy as np
got = answers['tok_emb[ids] + pos_emb[0]']
real = np.shape(tok_emb[ids] + pos_emb[0])
assert got is not None, 'fill in your prediction for tok_emb[ids] + pos_emb[0]'
assert tuple(got) == tuple(real), f'you predicted {got} but tok_emb[ids] + pos_emb[0] has shape {real}. Broadcasting: a (d,) row is added to every row of a (T, d) array, so the shape stays (T, d). (Every token would get position 0, which is a bug, but a silent one.)'

tests.name: shape of pos[:, None]
tests.code:
import numpy as np
got = answers['pos[:, None]']
real = np.shape(pos[:, None])
assert got is not None, 'fill in your prediction for pos[:, None]'
assert tuple(got) == tuple(real), f'you predicted {got} but pos[:, None] has shape {real}. Indexing with None inserts a new axis of length 1, turning (T,) into a column (T, 1).'

tests.name: shape of pos[:, None] * freq[None, :]
tests.code:
import numpy as np
got = answers['pos[:, None] * freq[None, :]']
real = np.shape(pos[:, None] * freq[None, :])
assert got is not None, 'fill in your prediction for pos[:, None] * freq[None, :]'
assert tuple(got) == tuple(real), f'you predicted {got} but pos[:, None] * freq[None, :] has shape {real}. (T, 1) times (1, d/2) broadcasts to (T, d/2): every position times every frequency. This is the angle table for sinusoidal encodings.'

hints: (T, d) + (d,) broadcasts the row to every one of the T rows.
(T, 1) * (1, k) gives (T, k): an outer product.

import numpy as np

V, d, T_max = 8, 6, 16
tok_emb = np.zeros((V, d))           # one row per token
pos_emb = np.zeros((T_max, d))       # one row per position
ids = np.array([3, 1, 4, 4, 0])      # a 5-token text
T = len(ids)
pos = np.arange(T)                   # positions 0..T-1
freq = np.ones(d // 2)               # one frequency per sine/cosine pair

# Predict each shape as a tuple, e.g. (4, 3), BEFORE printing anything.
# Then check yourself with print(<expression>.shape).
answers = {
    "tok_emb[ids]": (5, 6),
    "pos_emb[:T]": (5, 6),
    "tok_emb[ids] + pos_emb[:T]": (5, 6),
    "tok_emb[ids] + pos_emb[0]": (5, 6),
    "pos[:, None]": (5, 1),
    "pos[:, None] * freq[None, :]": (5, 3),
}

problems.title: Sinusoidal positional encoding
problems.prompt:
Write sinusoidal(T, d) from the original transformer paper:

PE[t, 2i] = sin(t / 10000**(2i/d))   and   PE[t, 2i+1] = cos(t / 10000**(2i/d))

Use broadcasting instead of loops: a column of positions (T, 1) times a row of frequencies (d/2,) gives the whole angle table at once. pe[:, 0::2] selects the even columns and pe[:, 1::2] the odd ones.
problems.starter:
import numpy as np

def sinusoidal(T, d):
    """Fixed positional encodings of the original transformer, shape (T, d), d even.
    PE[t, 2i] = sin(t / 10000**(2i/d)),  PE[t, 2i+1] = cos(t / 10000**(2i/d))"""
    pe = np.zeros((T, d))
    # TODO 1: pos = the positions 0..T-1 as a column, shape (T, 1)
    # TODO 2: freq = 1 / 10000**(2i/d) for i = 0 .. d/2 - 1, shape (d/2,)
    # TODO 3: angles = pos * freq   -> (T, d/2) by broadcasting
    # TODO 4: put np.sin(angles) in the even columns (pe[:, 0::2]) and np.cos(angles) in the odd ones (pe[:, 1::2])
    return pe

tests.name: shape
tests.code:
import numpy as np
out=sinusoidal(10,8)
assert out.shape==(10,8), f'expected (T, d) = (10, 8), got {out.shape}'

tests.name: position 0 is [0, 1, 0, 1, ...]
tests.code:
import numpy as np
out=sinusoidal(4,6)
assert np.allclose(out[0],[0,1,0,1,0,1]), f'at t = 0 every sin is 0 and every cos is 1, got {out[0].round(3)}'

tests.name: matches the formula
first pair is the fastest wave
tests.code:
import numpy as np
out=sinusoidal(3,8)
assert np.isclose(out[1,0],np.sin(1.0)), f'the first pair has frequency 1, so PE[1, 0] = sin(1) = {np.sin(1):.4f}; got {out[1,0]:.4f}'

tests.name: every position gets a different vector
tests.code:
import numpy as np
out=sinusoidal(50,16)
D=((out[:,None,:]-out[None,:,:])**2).sum(-1)+np.eye(50)
assert D.min()>1e-6, 'two positions got identical encodings'

hints: angles = pos * freq; pe[:, 0::2] = np.sin(angles); pe[:, 1::2] = np.cos(angles)
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

def sinusoidal(T, d):
    """Fixed positional encodings of the original transformer, shape (T, d), d even.
    PE[t, 2i] = sin(t / 10000**(2i/d)),  PE[t, 2i+1] = cos(t / 10000**(2i/d))"""
    pe = np.zeros((T, d))
    pos = np.arange(T)[:, None]
    freq = 1.0 / 10000 ** (np.arange(0, d, 2) / d)
    angles = pos * freq
    pe[:, 0::2] = np.sin(angles)
    pe[:, 1::2] = np.cos(angles)
    return pe

problems.title: Token plus position (GPT, step 6)
problems.prompt:
Our GPT uses learned positions, like GPT-2. Write gpt_inputs(ids, tok_emb, pos_emb) returning tok_emb[ids] + pos_emb[:T], and raise a ValueError when the text is longer than the position table (the model has no vector for those positions).

Reminder of the syntax: raise ValueError("message").

One test checks the payoff: the two ls in hello used to get identical vectors; with positions added they differ.
problems.starter:
import numpy as np

# ---- the character-level GPT so far (lessons 9.1 to 9.7) ----
text = "hello world"
vocab = sorted(set(text))
stoi = {ch: i for i, ch in enumerate(vocab)}
def encode(s):
    return [stoi[ch] for ch in s]

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
d, block_size = 8, 16                           # block_size: the longest context the model accepts
tok_emb = rng.normal(size=(len(vocab), d))      # (V, d)
pos_emb = rng.normal(size=(block_size, d))      # (block_size, d), learned like tok_emb

# ---- step 6: token + position (this lesson) ----
def gpt_inputs(ids, tok_emb, pos_emb):
    """(T,) token IDs -> (T, d) inputs: token embedding plus the position row for where each token sits.
    Raise a ValueError if the text is longer than the position table."""
    ids = np.asarray(ids)
    T = len(ids)
    # TODO 1: if T is larger than the number of rows in pos_emb, raise ValueError("text longer than block_size")
    # TODO 2: return tok_emb[ids] + pos_emb[:T]
    pass

tests.name: shape and value
tests.code:
import numpy as np
ids=encode('hello')
out=gpt_inputs(ids,tok_emb,pos_emb)
assert out is not None, 'gpt_inputs returned None'
assert out.shape==(5,8), f'expected (T, d) = (5, 8), got {out.shape}'
assert np.allclose(out,tok_emb[ids]+pos_emb[:5]), 'row t should be tok_emb[ids[t]] + pos_emb[t]'

tests.name: repeated characters now differ
tests.code:
import numpy as np
out=gpt_inputs(encode('hello'),tok_emb,pos_emb)
assert not np.allclose(out[2],out[3]), 'the two l characters sit at positions 2 and 3, so their inputs should differ'

tests.name: not every token gets position 0
tests.code:
import numpy as np
ids=encode('hello')
out=gpt_inputs(ids,tok_emb,pos_emb)
assert not np.allclose(out,tok_emb[ids]+pos_emb[0]), 'it looks like every token got pos_emb[0]: broadcasting hid the bug. Use pos_emb[:T].'

tests.name: too long raises ValueError
exactly block_size is fine
tests.code:
import numpy as np
out=gpt_inputs([0]*16,tok_emb,pos_emb)
assert out.shape==(16,8), 'a text of exactly block_size tokens should still work'

hints: T = len(ids); compare it with len(pos_emb).
if T > len(pos_emb): raise ValueError("text longer than block_size")
problems.solution:
import numpy as np

# ---- the character-level GPT so far (lessons 9.1 to 9.7) ----
text = "hello world"
vocab = sorted(set(text))
stoi = {ch: i for i, ch in enumerate(vocab)}
def encode(s):
    return [stoi[ch] for ch in s]

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
d, block_size = 8, 16                           # block_size: the longest context the model accepts
tok_emb = rng.normal(size=(len(vocab), d))      # (V, d)
pos_emb = rng.normal(size=(block_size, d))      # (block_size, d), learned like tok_emb

# ---- step 6: token + position (this lesson) ----
def gpt_inputs(ids, tok_emb, pos_emb):
    """(T,) token IDs -> (T, d) inputs: token embedding plus the position row for where each token sits.
    Raise a ValueError if the text is longer than the position table."""
    ids = np.asarray(ids)
    T = len(ids)
    if T > len(pos_emb):
        raise ValueError("text longer than block_size")
    return tok_emb[ids] + pos_emb[:T]
